items.followUp: Define zero error and explain how zero correction is applied to a measured reading.

rubric.why: Assesses the meaning of zero error.
rubric.description: Defines zero error as a non-zero reading when the actual quantity is zero.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the instrument shows a non-zero reading at the actual zero value.

rubric.why: Assesses the meaning and use of zero correction.
rubric.description: States that zero correction is opposite in sign to zero error and is added to the observed reading.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the correction's sign and how it is applied.

modelAnswer: Zero error is the non-zero reading shown by a measuring instrument when the actual value of the quantity being measured is zero.
Zero correction is equal in magnitude but opposite in sign to zero error; it is added to the observed reading.

items.followUp: A screw gauge has a pitch of 1 mm and 100 divisions on its circular scale. Find its least count.

rubric.why: Checks how the pitch of a screw gauge is determined.
rubric.description: States that pitch is the distance moved by the spindle in one complete rotation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing how to determine the pitch.

accept: number of divisions on the circular scale
rubric.description: Gives least count as pitch divided by the number of circular-scale divisions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula.

modelAnswer: Find the pitch: the distance moved by the spindle in one complete rotation.
Count the divisions on the circular scale.
Least count = pitch ÷ number of divisions on the circular scale.

items.followUp: Why must the direction of a force be considered when finding the resultant of two forces?

rubric.why: Checks the defining feature that distinguishes vectors from scalars.
rubric.description: States that a vector has both magnitude and direction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying both magnitude and direction.

rubric.why: Checks why ordinary scalar addition and subtraction are not sufficient.
rubric.description: Explains that directions must be considered and magnitudes alone cannot be combined like scalars.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that vector addition or subtraction must account for direction.

modelAnswer: Vector quantities have both magnitude and direction.
Therefore, their directions must be considered when adding or subtracting them; their magnitudes alone cannot be combined like scalar quantities.

items.followUp: State Newton's Second Law of Motion and write its equation in terms of momentum.

rubric.why: Checks the statement of Newton's Second Law.
rubric.description: States that the rate of change of momentum is directly proportional to the applied force and occurs in its direction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the law, including the direction of the change.

rubric.why: Checks the mathematical expression of the law.
rubric.description: Writes the momentum form of the equation or the constant-mass form.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either correct equation.

modelAnswer: Newton's Second Law states that the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of that force.
F = Δp/Δt; for constant mass, F = ma.

items.followUp: A force of 10 N acts at an angle to the horizontal. What is meant by resolving this force into components?

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of resolving a force.
rubric.description: Defines resolution as splitting a force into component forces in specified directions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining resolution in terms of components and their directions.

rubric.why: Checks the relationship between the components and the original force.
rubric.description: States that the components together have the same effect as the original force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the combined effect of the components.

modelAnswer: Resolution of forces is the process of splitting a force into component forces in specified directions.
The components together have the same effect as the original force.
